newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW - Bloomberg has no plans to go public.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Bloomberg has no plans to go public.

text.p: The founder and chairman of U.S. business information group Bloomberg LP said on Tuesday he had no plans to sell his majority stake in the company or float it on the stock exchange.
Nor does he plan to follow rivals Reuters Holdings Plc or Dow Jones and Co Inc, both publicly quoted, by buying other news outlets or distribution companies.
"We'll never go public. When will I sell the company? When it ceases to be fun. I am 55 and I see no reason why at age 60 it would not be fun," Bloomberg told Reuters in an interview.

Bloomberg, in London to promote his autobiography "Bloomberg by Bloomberg", said his company would grow organically and plough back its earnings -- estimated in U.S. press reports to be $200 million in 1996 -- into expanding "all sectors."
He said Bloomberg LP, owned 20 percent by Merrill Lynch and Co Inc, should increase sales by 30 percent in 1997 though he did not provide outright figures.

"In 1997 we have been growing (sales) at 30 percent a year and this year we have budgeted an increase in virtually every single division of the company - news, programming, data collection, sales, administration, installation, support -- of roughly a third," he said.
Bloomberg said he would continue to plough earnings back into company expansion and product development.
"I have always been a believer that we should grow by developing new products as opposed to acquiring."

Bloomberg said the company had come a long way from its start in 1981 when he spent $4 million of his own money to develop the Bloomberg delivery system which now is on 75,000 terminals world-wide. It employs about 3,500 people in 100 countries which Bloomberg laments is perhaps too big to continue for long the flat management structure he enjoys.

"I am fighting bureaucracy all the time. I think there is no reason why we can't continue to have this open structure and relatively flat management style that is very different from what a European company would do," he said.
He said he considers Reuters to be his company's biggest rival in the global financial news agency business but that Dow Jones had fallen to third place.
"We came in and they should have been watching what they were doing and never let it happen," Bloomberg said.
However he does not fret over what the competition is doing and focuses on customer feedback.

"We can't sit back and worry what either of those companies are doing. We have got to go ahead and improve our product and ask our customers and potential customers 'What would you like and how can we make it better'."

Bloomberg said he was not worried about competition from the Internet and saw it as a "big boom" to transmit his customers' information if "it becomes reliable enough and fast enough to have all of our customers come over it."
He said the company could save $100 million a year in long distance phone charges if all its customers received the feed from the Internet.
"But the Internet today is not fast enough and consistent enough to substitute our controlled dedicated network," he said.
However, Bloomberg aims to convert over the next two months to the Internet all its customers receiving its system through a dial-up modem.
"But the Internet is growing so fast...all of us will wind up using it," he said.
